young.html: Thomas Hobbes lived in England during a terrible civil war, when English people fought each other over who should rule. He asked a big question: why do we need a government at all?

Imagine a playground with no teachers and no rules. Anyone could grab your ball. You might start grabbing first, just to be safe. Everyone would be nervous all the time, and nobody would build anything, because it could be taken away. Hobbes called this the state of nature.

His answer: people agree with each other to give one ruler (a person or a group) the power to make rules and keep the peace. Then everyone can relax, work and build. He named his book after Leviathan, a huge sea creature in the Bible, because he thought the government had to be big and strong.

young.name: gb-leviathan
young.cap: Step from the state of nature, through the agreement, to the commonwealth.

young.html: Not everyone agreed with Hobbes. Later thinkers worried that a ruler with that much power could become a bully too. That argument goes on through the next rungs of this ladder.

The no-rules game. Play a simple game (cards, tag or building with blocks) for two minutes with no rules at all, then again with rules everyone agrees on and a referee. Talk about it: which was more fun? What did the referee need to be able to do? What would you do if the referee were unfair?

full.html: Thomas Hobbes (1588–1679) was a tutor and scholar who visited Galileo, met Descartes and wrote one of the Objections to Descartes's Meditations. Fearing for his safety as civil war approached, he went to Paris in 1640 and stayed for eleven years. Leviathan was published in London in 1651, just as the war ended. Hobbes wanted to build a science of politics the way Euclid built geometry: from definitions about human nature to conclusions about government.

full.text: Part I: human nature and the state of nature

full.html: Hobbes begins with sense, imagination, speech and the passions, and argues that people are roughly equal: even the weakest can kill the strongest by a plot or with allies. Equal people wanting the same things, with no one over them, have three causes of quarrel: competition (for gain), diffidence, his word for distrust (for safety), and glory (for reputation).

full.text: Hereby it is manifest that during the time men live without a common power to keep them all in awe, they are in that condition which is called war; and such a war as is of every man against every man.
full.author: Thomas Hobbes
full.ed: Andrew Crooke, London; spelling modernized in the Project Gutenberg text

full.html: By “war” Hobbes means not only fighting but a constant readiness to fight, as “foul weather” means not one shower but many days' inclination to rain. In such a condition, he says, nothing lasting can be built:

full.text: In such condition there is no place for industry, because the fruit thereof is uncertain: and consequently no culture of the earth; no navigation, nor use of the commodities that may be imported by sea; no commodious building; no instruments of moving and removing such things as require much force; no knowledge of the face of the earth; no account of time; no arts; no letters; no society; and which is worst of all, continual fear, and danger of violent death; and the life of man, solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short.
full.author: Thomas Hobbes
full.ed: Andrew Crooke, London; spelling modernized in the Project Gutenberg text

full.text: The laws of nature and the covenant

full.html: Reason, Hobbes says, finds laws of nature: rules for keeping alive. The first: seek peace when you can, and defend yourself when you cannot. The second: be willing to give up your right to all things, if others will do the same. The third: keep the agreements you make, which he calls the root of justice. But agreements without power to enforce them are only words. So people covenant with one another to hand their right of governing themselves to one sovereign, a single person or an assembly, who will keep the peace for all.

full.name: gb-leviathan
full.cap: Hobbes's argument in three stages. The sovereign may be one person or an assembly.

full.text: Part II: the powers of the sovereign

full.html: Hobbes gives the sovereign great powers: to make and judge the laws, to decide on war and peace, to choose officers and to judge which teachings may be taught. He argues that dividing these powers invites the very civil war he had lived through. Yet subjects keep some rights: no one can be bound to give up the right to defend his own life, and when the sovereign can no longer protect them, their duty of obedience ends.

Hobbes's key move: authority comes from the agreement of the people, made for their own safety, not from tradition or from a claim that kings rule by divine right. Many royalists disliked this as much as his opponents disliked his strong sovereign.

Parts III and IV, about half the book, discuss the Bible, the church and religious authority. Hobbes argues that in a Christian commonwealth the sovereign, not a separate church power, has the final say on public religion. These parts were among the most controversial in his own time.

Reading Hobbes as saying people are simply wicked. His point is that even reasonable people, with no common power to trust, are driven by fear and distrust to strike first. Change the situation, he argues, and behavior changes.

deep.text: Critics and how history judged him

deep.html: Hobbes was attacked from many sides. Churchmen accused him of unbelief because of his views on the soul and on church authority, and Parliament discussed Leviathan in an inquiry into irreligious books in 1666; Hobbes himself professed to be a Christian. Royalists objected that he founded the king's power on consent. In the next era, John Locke answered that people in a state of nature already have rights given by natural law, that government's power is limited by its purpose, and that a government that violates those rights may be resisted. Rousseau objected that Hobbes's “natural” man was really a person already shaped by society.

Historians of thought generally rank Leviathan as a founding work of modern political philosophy and of social contract theory. His case for a single, undivided sovereign was largely rejected by later constitutional thinkers, who divided and limited power (see Montesquieu and The Federalist in the next era). His starting points, human equality, consent and security, were widely adopted, including by many who reached opposite conclusions.

items: Is safety the main purpose of government, or one purpose among several?
Can a government strong enough to protect everyone be kept from abusing its power? How?
Do people behave well mostly because of rules, or for other reasons too?

questions: Hobbes says that without rules, people might grab first out of fear. Do you think that's true? Can you think of times people cooperated with no rules at all?
What rules does your family have that keep the peace? Who decides them, and how?
Hobbes lived through a civil war. How might that experience have shaped what he wrote?
Is it fair for one person or group to have the final say? What would make it fairer?
Hobbes says a promise nobody can enforce is “only words.” Do you agree?
